clue.text: Retort apportioning blame I'm beginning to challenge

indicators.note: apportioning means dividing up and sharing out, so the letters of blame are parcelled out anew
beginning to applies to both following words, taking the opening letter of I'm and of challenge

explanation.surface: Someone answers an accusation by sharing out the blame, and starts by challenging it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apportioning' rearranges BLAME into ALEMB; 'beginning to' then takes the first letters of 'I'm' and 'challenge', IC. 'Retort' looks like a sharp reply but is the chemist's distilling vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are glass vessels used by old chemists and alchemists for distilling liquids.

clue.text: Summary of article copyright in Peru

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

indicators.note: in means the copyright letter sits inside the country name

parts.note: C, in a circle, is the copyright symbol

explanation.surface: A summary of an article concerning copyright law in Peru.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts C, the copyright symbol, inside PERU, after A.
explanation.definitionFit: A French borrowing for a brief outline or insight, a quick summing-up.

clue.text: In which Othello, being wrought, was perplexed

definitions.text: In which Othello, being wrought, was perplexed

parts.words: In which Othello, being wrought, was perplexed
parts.note: quotes Othello's last speech, in which he calls himself one not easily jealous but, being wrought, perplexed to the utmost degree

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare about the agitated Moor.
explanation.walkthrough: The final word of Shakespeare's line 'Perplexed in the ...' is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello says he was perplexed to the utmost degree, which is what the phrase with the answer means.

clue.text: No escape from star's death here in Fort William?

definitions.text: No escape from star's death here

explanation.surface: Asks whether a place of no escape lies inside an old fort.
explanation.walkthrough: Fort William in Calcutta housed the notorious 1756 dungeon of that name; the astronomical sense is a collapsed star from which not even light escapes.
explanation.definitionFit: A collapsed dead star whose gravity lets nothing out; and the cramped prison cell in Calcutta's fort.

clue.text: Accompanying officer and other rank with German worker

parts.note: CO is commanding officer
an NCO, non-commissioned officer, is one of the other ranks rather than a commissioned officer
mit is German for with
an ant is the usual crossword worker

explanation.surface: An officer and a soldier of lower rank go along with a German labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with German' is a single piece: the German word for with.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that goes along with or naturally attends something else is said to accompany it.

clue.text: Impressionable sort of surgeon

explanation.surface: A doctor described as easily swayed, a type of surgeon.
explanation.definitionFit: A substance that can be moulded easily takes impressions; a cosmetic surgeon who reshapes bodies is the other sort named.

clue.text: Room for a launch?

explanation.surface: Asks whether there is a room for a launch party.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for one's flat or living room; and a rocket's lift-off platform.

clue.text: Current increase may give trouble

parts.note: read as electricity, a surge in current turned up makes things misbehave; current is AC, raised

explanation.surface: A power surge in the electricity supply could cause problems.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer means misbehave; it also reads as AC (alternating current) plus a turned-up T.
explanation.definitionFit: To misbehave or malfunction, as children or machines do when causing problems.

clue.text: A tour he made for US author

indicators.note: made signals that the letters of a tour he are made into something new

explanation.surface: A man takes a trip in honour of an American writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made' rearranges A TOUR HE.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry David, the nineteenth-century American who wrote Walden.

clue.text: Island contains nothing so antiseptic

indicators.note: contains says the island's letters go round the rest

parts.note: Crete is a Greek island
O, the figure nought, is nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: An island has nothing in it, so it is completely sterile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contains' wraps the Greek island round the letter for nothing and the word so as written; 'antiseptic' is the definition, not a description of the island.
explanation.definitionFit: A coal-tar oil used as a wood preservative and formerly as a disinfectant.

clue.text: Fuse, included in case of possible need, put on board

indicators.note: included in the case of means held inside the letters that follow
possible signals one possible arrangement of the letters of need

parts.note: a train is a line of gunpowder laid as a fuse to set off a charge

explanation.surface: A fuse is packed just in case it is needed and loaded aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possible' rearranges the four letters of need into ENED; 'Fuse' is a gunpowder train, which 'included in case of' places inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: To board a railway carriage, or to load troops onto one, is the verb formed from the rail vehicle.

clue.text: Irony, for example, right out of place in a drunk

indicators.note: out of place says the letter for right shifts to a new position within the word

parts.note: a toper is a habitual heavy drinker

explanation.surface: Being drunk and in the wrong place is described as a kind of irony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of place' moves the R of TOPER, a drunkard, one place forward to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Irony is a figure of speech, a non-literal use of language, which is what this rhetorical term names.

clue.text: Club or coterie, say

indicators.note: say signals that the word is spoken, the sound standing in for the spelling

parts.note: a coterie is an exclusive little circle of people, a clique

explanation.surface: Asks whether a club is the same thing as an exclusive set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' gives a word sounding like CLIQUE. 'Club' is the golf sense: an old iron-headed golf club, chiefly Scottish.
explanation.definitionFit: An old Scottish golfing iron, roughly a driving iron or long iron.

clue.text: Squatters could be precious cheeky at first

indicators.note: could be signals that the letters could be rearranged into something else
at first takes only the opening letter of cheeky

explanation.surface: People squatting in a building might be described as rather precious and cheeky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' gives C from 'cheeky'; 'could be' rearranges PRECIOUS plus C.
explanation.definitionFit: Squatters are people living in property they have taken over without owning it, i.e. residents in possession.

clue.text: Secret tribe set apart

parts.note: a clan is a tribe or extended family group
to destine is to set apart or assign for a purpose

explanation.surface: A secretive tribe keeps itself apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Done covertly, hidden from view.

clue.text: First instalment of story provides interest

definitions.note: the definition describes the answer, a bank holding that pays interest, by what it does

parts.note: a deposit is the first part payment made when buying something
an account is a narrative or report of events

explanation.surface: The opening part of a serial story is gripping enough to hold the reader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interest' reads as reader engagement but is the money a bank pays on savings.
explanation.definitionFit: A savings arrangement at a bank in which money left on deposit earns a return.

clue.text: Punch, so-called, making a rich variety — not yet stirred

indicators.note: not says some letters are excluded from the pool
stirred says the remaining letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A punch is made from a rich mix of ingredients that hasn't been stirred yet.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the letters of YET from A RICH VARIETY ('not yet') and 'stirred' rearranges the rest. Punch magazine was subtitled The London Charivari.
explanation.definitionFit: Punch, the satirical British magazine, bore this word as its subtitle; it means a noisy mock serenade.

clue.text: Applaud separate rising? Nonsense!

parts.note: to clap is to applaud

indicators.note: rising means the word reads upwards in this down entry, so backwards

parts.note: to part is to separate

explanation.surface: An audience rises and applauds, then the speaker dismisses the ovation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns PART into TRAP.
explanation.definitionFit: Pretentious empty talk, meant only to win applause.

clue.text: Comedians with strange allure and bold with it

indicators.note: strange signals that the letters of allure are made odd, rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
hardy means bold, daring

explanation.surface: A pair of comics are odd, alluring and daring, and very up to date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges ALLURE; 'with it' only links. The answer is the classic film double act Stan and Ollie.
explanation.definitionFit: Stan and Oliver were a famous comic double act of early Hollywood films.

clue.text: Destroys original character of Unionism, with footnote about radical

indicators.note: original character of means the first letter of the word
about means the footnote letters go round the other piece

parts.note: PS, postscript, is a note added at the foot of a letter
a root is a radical in mathematics and grammar

explanation.surface: Someone wrecks the founding spirit of Unionism by adding a note about a radical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'original character of' takes the first letter of Unionism; 'about' wraps the postscript abbreviation round a root, which is a radical in maths.
explanation.definitionFit: To tear out by the roots is to destroy completely or eradicate.

clue.text: Girl gets more pay to keep records

parts.note: Di is a girl's name, short for Diana
a rise is British for an increase in pay, so 'a rise'

explanation.surface: A young woman receives a pay increase to maintain the files.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a pay increase is a rise (American: raise).
explanation.definitionFit: To record events in a daily journal.

clue.text: Put up money for a junket

definitions.note: the definition describes the answer by its use in making the dessert

indicators.note: put up means written upwards in this down entry, so backwards

parts.note: a tenner is a ten-pound note

explanation.surface: Someone puts up money to pay for a free trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' reverses TENNER, British slang for a ten-pound note. Junket is a sweet milk dessert set with this curdling agent, not a jolly.
explanation.definitionFit: The curdling extract from a calf's stomach is used to set milk into the dessert.

clue.text: Camp-followers at airborne stations?

explanation.surface: Hangers-on hanging round the bases of airborne troops.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as a short word for a paratrooper plus places, and it gives positions for airborne soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Hangers-on who live off others, like those trailing an army; and, split, the locations for parachute troops.

clue.text: Schoolboy detailed to follow game

indicators.note: detailed means with its tail cut off, so the final letter goes

parts.note: Stalky is the schoolboy hero of Kipling's Stalky & Co

explanation.surface: A schoolboy is given detailed orders to tail a sporting match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' cuts the last letter from STALKY, Kipling's schoolboy.
explanation.definitionFit: To pursue prey stealthily, as hunters do deer.

clue.text: Furious, that is, about 'art nouveau'

indicators.note: about means going round, so the other letters are placed around the middle part

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

indicators.note: nouveau is French for new, so the letters of art are given a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is furious about Art Nouveau.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nouveau', French for new, gives the three art letters a new order, and 'about' wraps the i.e. abbreviation round them.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone in a fury, very angry.

clue.text: In Brazil Germans say yes to Spanish wine

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro is a city in Brazil
ja is German for yes

explanation.surface: German tourists in Brazil agree to drink a Spanish wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A red wine from the region of northern Spain of the same name.

clue.text: Copy a form of flattery

explanation.surface: Copying is said to be a kind of flattery.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says this is the sincerest form of flattery.
explanation.definitionFit: A copy or replica; and the thing a proverb calls the sincerest compliment.

clue.text: Fashionable name of Austrian flower

definitions.note: flower is crosswordese for a river, something that flows

parts.note: in means fashionable

explanation.surface: A fashionable name for an Alpine bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is something that flows, a river: this one flows through Innsbruck in Austria.
explanation.definitionFit: The river that runs through Innsbruck, Austria's Tyrol, into the Danube.

clue.text: Nepotistic Russian author?

parts.note: a nepotist promotes or advances relations, and two words meaning promote and relatives together name a famous Russian poet

explanation.surface: Asks about a Russian writer who favours relatives.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Russian poet of Eugene Onegin, whose name splits into words for promoting one's relatives.

clue.text: Strachey's Australian statesmen?

parts.note: Lytton Strachey wrote a book of biographies of distinguished Victorians; people of the state of Victoria are Australian statesmen in a punning sense

explanation.surface: Asks which Australian politicians Lytton Strachey wrote about.
explanation.walkthrough: Strachey's book title is the answer followed by Victorians; Victoria is an Australian state, so its citizens are 'statesmen' in the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: The first word of Strachey's book title means distinguished, famous.
